clue.text: Unable to supply card that's so unusual

parts.note: a shop that is out of something is unable to supply it
a card is an eccentric person, a real character

explanation.surface: A dealer cannot produce a particular card, which is most unlike them.
explanation.walkthrough: 'card' looks like a playing card but is the old slang for an odd, amusing person.
explanation.definitionFit: Behaviour said to be out of character is unusual or untypical for the person concerned.

clue.text: Where grave words may be spoken? No fear!

definitions.text: Where grave words may be spoken?

explanation.surface: Words spoken at a graveside, and a defiant refusal.
explanation.walkthrough: The first reading is cryptic: words said at a funeral are spoken over a dead body; the second is the emphatic refusal.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an idiom of absolute refusal, and literally where a funeral oration might be delivered.

clue.text: After checking, mark as free from parasite

explanation.surface: Someone ticks a list item once a creature has been cleared of parasites.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense is cryptic: to tick off an animal would be to remove its ticks, bloodsucking parasites.
explanation.definitionFit: To tick off is to mark items as checked; whimsically, a dog freed of ticks has been ticked off.

clue.text: Criticism unknown for such pastry

parts.note: flak is hostile criticism, from anti-aircraft fire
Y is an algebraic unknown, like X and Z

explanation.surface: A baker faces criticism over a pastry no one recognises.
explanation.definitionFit: Flaky pastry is the kind made in thin crumbly layers, so the adjective describes such pastry.

clue.text: Producing rabbits, perhaps, and instantly dispatching several?

explanation.surface: A conjuror pulling rabbits out and a bowler removing batsmen in quick succession.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket a bowler who takes three wickets with three successive balls achieves this feat; a conjuror pulls rabbits from a top hat.
explanation.definitionFit: A magician's classic trick is with a hat, and in cricket the term means three wickets in consecutive balls.

clue.text: Part of build-up of arms, some distance from centre

explanation.surface: A military build-up of weapons spreading out some distance from a centre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'arms' suggests weapons but means the body's arms, whose forearm contains this bone.
explanation.definitionFit: The radius is one of the two forearm bones, and in geometry a line from a circle's centre to its edge.

clue.text: Man of straw is feebly funny, captivating pretty girl

indicators.note: captivating means holding prisoner, so one word is put around the other

parts.note: a corny joke is feebly funny, hackneyed
doll is old slang for a pretty girl

explanation.surface: A scarecrow-like figure tells weak jokes while charming a pretty girl.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Man of straw' usually means a sham or weak person; here it is literal, a figure woven from straw.
explanation.definitionFit: A corn dolly is a figure woven from straw at harvest, literally a little man of straw.

clue.text: Each short afternoon nap makes one most relaxed

indicators.note: short means cut down, so letters are dropped from both words that follow and precede it

parts.note: taken as written, before shortening
a siesta is an afternoon nap in hot countries

explanation.surface: A brief afternoon nap every day leaves one wonderfully relaxed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'short' trims EACH to EA and SIESTA to SIEST, losing CH and the final A.
explanation.definitionFit: Easiest is the superlative of easy in the sense of relaxed and unworried.

clue.text: Fruitless race to reach Canada, say

definitions.text: Fruitless race to reach Canada, say

parts.words: Fruitless race to reach Canada, say
parts.note: a pointless pursuit, read literally as chasing an untamed bird of the Canada kind

explanation.surface: A doomed race to get to Canada.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Canada' looks like the country but is the Canada goose, an example of a wild bird being chased.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom names a fruitless pursuit of something unattainable, literally hunting an untamed bird.

clue.text: Trenchant editor not altogether delighted by spelling

indicators.note: not altogether says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A sharp-tongued editor is only partly pleased with a writer's spelling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spelling' looks like orthography but means casting a spell.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone enchanted is under a spell, delighted as if by magic.

clue.text: Baronet taken aback, greeting holy man

indicators.note: taken aback here means turned back to front, so the title is reversed

parts.note: a baronet is addressed as Sir
hi is an informal greeting

explanation.surface: A startled baronet says hello to a holy man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taken aback' looks like surprise but turns SIR into RIS.
explanation.definitionFit: A rishi is a Hindu sage or saint, an inspired holy man.

clue.text: Low, deplorably heartless and sullen

parts.note: to low is to moo, as cattle do

indicators.note: heartless means the inner letters are removed, leaving only the first and last

explanation.surface: Feeling low and wretchedly cold, someone becomes sullen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Low' looks like an adjective for mood but is the verb for a cow's call.
explanation.definitionFit: Moody and sullen are near synonyms for gloomy, bad-tempered behaviour.

clue.text: No squaring up by this old soldier?

definitions.text: No squaring up by this old soldier?

parts.words: No squaring up by this old soldier?
parts.note: an English Civil War Parliamentarian, named for cropped hair, whose top is curved rather than square

explanation.surface: An old soldier refuses to square up for a fight.
explanation.walkthrough: Parliamentarian soldiers in the English Civil War were nicknamed for their close-cropped hair; a round head is literally not square at the top.
explanation.definitionFit: Roundheads were Cromwell's Parliamentarian soldiers, so a historical, old soldier.

clue.text: Successive notes intended for Opposition

parts.note: D and E are consecutive notes of the musical scale
one's intended is one's betrothed, a fiance

explanation.surface: A series of notes is meant for the opposition party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'intended' looks like a verb but is the noun for a husband-to-be.
explanation.definitionFit: Defiance is open resistance, a form of opposition.

clue.text: Tongue used in Africa and Asia Frank translated

indicators.note: translated means changed into another form, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A language spoken in Africa and Asia is translated by Frank.
explanation.walkthrough: 'translated' fits the language surface but rearranges ASIA FRANK.
explanation.definitionFit: Afrikaans is a language derived from Dutch, spoken in South Africa and Namibia.

clue.text: A disgrace to get very drunk

parts.note: a blot is a stain on one's reputation, a disgrace
taken as written

explanation.surface: It is shameful to get extremely drunk.
explanation.definitionFit: Blotto is informal for being extremely drunk.

clue.text: Peak of success, investing pounds in small boat

indicators.note: in, after investing, places the money symbol inside the vessel

parts.note: a pinnace is a small boat carried by a ship
L stands for pounds sterling, from Latin libra

explanation.surface: Success peaks when one invests money in a little boat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'investing pounds in' puts L inside PINNACE, before its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A pinnacle is the highest point, the peak of achievement.

clue.text: Declare a lock should turn the other way

indicators.note: turning the other way means reading the word for a curl backwards

parts.note: a lock of hair is a tress

explanation.surface: Someone says a door lock ought to turn in the opposite direction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lock' suggests a door but is a lock of hair; reversed it gives SSERT.
explanation.definitionFit: To assert is to declare something firmly.

clue.text: Like highlights from addressee of Irish journal, right?

parts.note: Jonathan Swift, the Irish writer, wrote the Journal to Stella, letters to Esther Johnson

explanation.surface: Highlights taken from letters to an Irish journal's reader, correct?
explanation.walkthrough: 'highlights' are stars, the outstanding people or things.
explanation.definitionFit: Stellar means starry, outstanding, like the star performers or highlights of a show.

clue.text: He kept rolling up, panicking shy puss I homed

indicators.note: panicking means agitated and confused, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A frightened shy cat comes home in a panic.
explanation.walkthrough: In Greek myth Sisyphus was condemned to roll a boulder up a hill forever. 'homed' is a link word, the anagram homing in on him.
explanation.definitionFit: The mythical king was punished by endlessly pushing a rock uphill, only for it to roll back.

clue.text: Destitute man's refuge, scripture

parts.note: a haven is a place of refuge
OT is the Old Testament, part of scripture

explanation.surface: A poor man's shelter is in holy writ.
explanation.definitionFit: A have-not is a person without wealth, someone destitute.

clue.text: Approving dull appearance of magazine

parts.note: to be for something is to approve of it
mat, or matt, means dull, not glossy

explanation.surface: Someone approves of a magazine's dull look.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dull' hints at a boring magazine but is the matt finish.
explanation.definitionFit: A magazine's format is its layout, size and general appearance.

clue.text: As result of mental stress, in analysis?

explanation.surface: Stress-related problems examined in analysis.
explanation.walkthrough: 'analysis' looks like psychoanalysis, but it is a breakdown of figures into parts.
explanation.definitionFit: A breakdown is both a mental collapse under stress and an itemised analysis.

clue.text: About the same numbers of Romans concerned with town administration

parts.note: C is short for circa, about
IV and I are Roman numerals, four and one
the same letter again, so a second C as for about

explanation.surface: Roughly as many Romans were involved in running a town.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole answer is made of Roman numerals and reads the same backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Civic means relating to a city or town and its administration.

clue.text: Army unit's anxiety to protect duke

indicators.note: protecting means enclosing, so one word wraps around the abbreviation

parts.note: care is worry or anxiety

explanation.surface: An army unit worries about guarding a duke.
explanation.definitionFit: A cadre is a core group of military personnel forming a unit.

clue.text: Mouth a letter

explanation.surface: A spoken letter, as from the mouth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mouth' is a river mouth; and delta is the Greek letter D.
explanation.definitionFit: A delta is a river's fan-shaped mouth and also the fourth Greek letter.

clue.text: Amid ocean? Wrong — it's landlocked

indicators.note: wrong means incorrect, so the letters are put in a different order

explanation.surface: Placing it in mid-ocean is wrong, since the country has no coast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Amid ocean' sounds like a location but is the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Macedonia, now North Macedonia, is a Balkan state with no coastline.

clue.text: Boldly confront likelihood of stingy response?

explanation.surface: Facing up to things boldly may provoke a stinging reply.
explanation.walkthrough: The second reading is cryptic: grabbing a stinging plant invites a painful response.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means to tackle a difficulty boldly; literally, seizing a stinging plant.
